Token Board Book

Build and print the four-page token board book: a Choices page (what the student is earning), a Teaching Targets page (the skill or replacement behavior being taught), the student’s own Board (First, Then, and the token slots) and a Tokens page where the token cards park, each with its instruction text on the back, plus the picture cards and tokens to cut out. Laminated and bound on the left, with the tabs on the right. Pictures come from the shared pictogram library or from photos you upload.

Nothing is stored in the browser. Entries live in this open window only until you save a file; close the tab and they are gone. Save to the district drive, not a personal device.

Token Board Book
Form TK-1 · Revised September 2026 · Printed

The Student and the Book

The Bus Ride

A token board for the ride: the bus rules are the cards on the Targets page (two to five; seatbelt on, stay in your seat, quiet voice, hands to self), the item to earn is a Choices card, and the tokens come at checkpoints along the route. Type the ride’s usual length; the form works out when each token comes, and prints a ride plan for the bus staff.

The length from Maps (optional)

To find the ride’s length, type the two addresses and tap Open in Maps: the Maps app on this device shows the driving time, and you type the minutes above (a school bus with its stops usually takes longer than a car; ask the transportation office for the route’s time if you can). The addresses are kept only in this file. The form never sends them anywhere, never prints them, and leaves them out of the CSV; Maps receives them only when you tap the button. Leave them blank and type the minutes if you prefer.

Landmarks along the route

Once the board works with the timer, the checkpoints can become things your learner sees from the window: a store, a park, a fire station, a bridge. List them in the order the bus passes them, with the minute each is passed; a picture helps a learner who does not read (a photo of the real place is best). Steps 2 and 3 use them; Step 1 ignores them.

#PictureLandmarkMinutes into the ride

Tokens

A terminal token: when the last token looks different, the learner can see which one finishes the board and that the item comes next. The Board’s last slot and the last box on the Tokens page get the same orange ring, and the token sheet prints one last token among the others.

The captions are written for the count: “Your First Star!”, “Keep Going!”, then “Just k More!” down to one. Edit any of them; changing the count or the token name writes them again.

What to Print, and in What Order

Duplex. The backs are the reverse of the fronts, so print the duplex order on a printer set to two-sided, flip on the long edge (landscape sheets, bound on the short edge; some drivers call it “long-edge binding”). Test one sheet first: the front’s tab is on the right and its back’s tab comes out on the left of the same sheet, at the same height. If the back comes out upside down, the driver is flipping on the short edge.

Size. The book page is 8.82 by 5.82 in, the trimmed size of the assessor’s bound books (every measurement comes from the Illustrator files). It prints centred on Letter landscape with trim marks at the four corners: cut 1.09 in off the left and the right and 1.34 in off the top and the bottom of every sheet (a Board with six to ten tokens is taller, 7.46 in: cut 0.52 in top and bottom). The 11 in wide page is the same page enlarged to the full width: cut 0.62 in off the top and the bottom. “Fill the Letter page” needs no cutting: only the white space between the elements grows. Print at 100%, not “fit to page”: the cards are cut to sit exactly in the boxes. The binding margin is the panel’s own inset on the bound side. Card sheets are full Letter.

Long backs. The text of a back is set at the files’ 12.3 pt (15.3 pt on the 11 in page) and never below 11 pt, with 3 percent kept in hand so a page that fits on screen also fits on paper. On the Token Economy back the credit line gives way first: it drops to one small line at the foot. What still does not fit continues on a second back page (in a duplex order a blank sheet is added first so every back stays on the reverse of its front).

Spares. The sheet of one card prints a portrait Letter page of that card repeated with cut lines, 5 across at about 1.5 in or 6 across at about 1.25 in: the smaller sizes are the samples’ own; a Letter sheet holds 6 or 7 rows of them.

Choices: What Are You Earning?

Six picture cards of the student’s preferred items. They park on the Choices page; the student picks one and it moves to the Then box on the Board. The reinforcer menu from Form PA-1 fills an empty list through “From the case” on the toolbar, or Form TE-1’s backups do, when linked (Setup). A card’s label prints above its picture, underlined; the picture’s own name is used when the label is blank. The card sheet adds an “Other” card with lines to write on.

Tap the pictures in the order you want them; they fill cards 1 to 6. To change one card, tap Choose on its row. The arrows move a card up or down.
#PictureLabel on the card

Targets: First, Teaching Targets

Six picture cards of the skills or replacement behaviors being taught; the chosen one moves to the First box on the Board (or the first ones with pictures form the row of a Rules-row Board). The case’s replacement behaviors and acquisition objectives fill an empty list through “From the case”; Form TE-1’s behavior can go on a card when the book is linked with it (Setup) and you tick it. Labels print above the picture, not underlined, as in the samples.

Tap the pictures in the order you want them; they fill cards 1 to 6. To change one card, tap Choose on its row. The arrows move a card up or down.
#PictureLabel on the card

The Board

The student’s photo in both top corners (one, at the top right, on the Rules-row layout), “First” over a grey box and “Then” over a green box, and the token slots along the bottom. Leave the First and Then boxes empty for the cards, or choose a picture to print in a box as a fixed preset (the picture then prints as a card inside the box).

The Instruction Backs

The text on the back of each page, in the assessor’s words. Markup: **bold**, *italic*, __underlined__, ## a centred heading; a blank line starts a paragraph; {n} prints the token count in words (and {n}th its ordinal: the fifth) and {token}, {tokens} and {TOKENS} the token’s name; {last} (on the Token Board back and in Step 3) prints one sentence about the last token when Setup makes it look different, and nothing when it does not. Long text is set smaller to fit the page.

How to use: the insert

Three steps in the assessor’s words, printed as a two-page insert after the backs when ticked on Setup (Steps 1 and 2 on the first page, Step 3 on the second). The first line of each block is its heading.

A narrated walkthrough of the four pages and one session, drawn from this book: its pictures, photo, colours and tokens. Play starts it with the sound on; the chapters jump to a step, and full screen fills the iPad. Space plays and pauses; the arrow keys skip five seconds.

Transcript of the narration

What This Form Makes

A token board book: four laminated landscape pages bound along the left edge, each with a coloured tab on the right so the four show when the book is closed. The Choices page (“What Are You Earning?”) holds six picture cards of the things the student likes; the Targets page (“First: Teaching Targets”) holds six cards of the skills or replacement behaviors being taught; the Board carries the student’s photo, a First box and a Then box, and a strip of token slots; the Tokens page is where the token cards wait. The back of each page carries its instructions. The adult puts the chosen target card under First and the chosen reward card under Then; the student earns tokens one at a time into the slots and, when the strip is full, gets what is under Then.

The arrangement is the Premack principle made visible (Premack, 1959): access to the more probable, preferred activity is made contingent on the less preferred one, which is what “First, then” says. The tokens are a token reinforcement system (Hackenberg, 2018): the token is a conditioned reinforcer earned on a token-production schedule and exchanged, when the strip is full, for the backup reinforcer under Then. Form TE-1 designs the schedules (how much work earns a token, how many tokens earn the exchange) and Form VS-1 prints the simpler strips; this form prints the book itself.

Linked forms. The band Link with Form TE-1 on Setup pairs this book with Form TE-1, the token economy plan for the same student. It is off until you turn it on, and an unlinked book saves and prints as before. Once it is on, Compare (in the workstation) or Open a file Form TE-1 saved (with this form on its own) sets the book beside the plan: a target card beside the behavior the tokens are earned for, the token count beside tokens per exchange, the token beside the token form, the Choices beside the backup menu, and the Token Economy back beside the schedule. The student’s name and ID are checked first. A compare only reads: nothing changes until you tick items and press Take the ticked items, and Undo what was just taken puts the book back as it was, until anything else changes. Form TE-1 is the plan of record, so its count, backups and schedule come ticked where they fill an empty place or have changed on the plan (the schedule paragraph is ticked by hand the first time, since it changes the printed back, and the row says beforehand whether that back then runs on to a second page). The plan’s behavior goes on a target card only when you tick it, and the card keeps its picture. It is not offered at all when it names a behavior to reduce: one of Form TB-1’s problem behaviors, which this book can check only while the workstation holds the case (or once a compare there has noted them), or a common word for one, such as aggression or elopement. With this form on its own and no case, check that the plan’s behavior is one to increase before you take it. A card taken onto, or kept with, the plan’s behavior is paired with it; a tap on a card number only chooses the card the table shows. The pictures, the token and the last-token marking are this book’s own, so a different token on the plan is offered unticked. Nothing is emptied or deleted, and a count change replaces edited captions only after asking. A backup the plan records as not a reinforcer (RA-1) is never offered, and class, cost and preference stay on Form TE-1. After a take, the panel names the pages to reprint until you press These pages are reprinted. Form TE-1 carries the same panel; it reads this book’s cards only while the link is on here, from a short summary the book keeps in its saved file.

Making the Book

1. Fill the pagesSetup: the student, the first name as it prints, the photo, the token count and picture (and, if you want one, a last token that looks different: the terminal token), the colours and the QR link. Choices and Targets: six pictures each, from the library or the student’s own photos (upload them through the picker). Choose all six pictures at once opens the picker on Several at once: tap the pictures in order (each shows its number), then Put them on the cards; Choose on one row changes that card, and the arrows move a card up or down. The two photos on the Board face each other: the right one is mirrored, as in the samples, or the left one, or neither (Setup). Board: leave First and Then empty for the cards, or set a fixed picture. Backs: the text is the assessor’s and can be edited. The simulator on the toolbar fills a sample student so the book can be seen at once.
2. PrintChoose the order on Setup. Fronts only gives the four pages; fronts and backs interleaves them for a duplex printer (two-sided, flip on the long edge; test one sheet); card sheets prints the choices, the targets and the tokens with cut lines; all prints everything; a sheet of one card prints spares. Print at 100%. From a computer every page is landscape Letter except the spare sheet, which is portrait. From an iPad or iPhone, Safari prints only portrait, so each book page is printed turned on its side on a portrait sheet at full size, and the card sheets are laid out portrait (cards at the 11 in size can take a second sheet); Setup’s Sheets can force either way. In each case the book page (8.82 by 5.82 in, or 11 in wide) is centred with trim marks, and Setup says how much to cut off.
3. Laminate and cutLaminate the four pages and the card sheets (5 mil or thicker pouches hold up). Cut the cards on the cut lines, rounding the corners a little so they do not catch.
4. Hook-and-loop dotsPut the hook side on every circle guide (the six boxes on Choices and on Targets, the First and Then boxes, the token slots, the token park boxes) and the loop side on the back of every card and token, so the cards do not catch on clothing.
5. BindPunch and bind along the left edge (spiral or comb) in the order Choices, Targets, Board, Tokens; the backs fall in place. The binding margin is already on the pages.
6. Teach itMake the tokens worth something first, as the Token Economy back says, and keep at it until the student reaches for the token: give a token and exchange it at once for the backup reinforcer (sampling); prompt the target response, give the token and exchange it at once (coaching); give the token right after the target response, exchange it at once, then begin to ask for more tokens before each exchange (conditioning). The check that it worked is that the behavior earning tokens goes up. Decide the schedule before starting (the “Not So FAST” paragraph on the Token Board back): a token after each response for a new skill, raised a little at a time as the skill holds, and back one step if the behavior falls apart (ratio strain). Keep the item under Then out of reach at other times, or the board loses its pull. The schedules are written on Form TE-1.

The Bus Ride (v21.49)

Book type at the top of Setup makes this a bus-ride book: a token board that rides along with the student and that the bus staff use the same way on every trip. The bus rules are the cards on the Targets page (two to five; staying in the seat, a quiet voice, hands to self; a rule with no picture in the library can be a photo or a word card), the item is a Choices card, picked before the ride and put in the Earn box, and the Board’s title reads “Sam’s Bus Chart”. The tokens come at checkpoints along the route instead of at the end of a classroom interval.

The ride’s lengthType the usual ride in minutes. To look it up, open The length from Maps, type the two addresses and tap Open in Maps: the Maps app on this device shows the driving time (a school bus with its stops usually takes longer than a car; the transportation office can give the route’s own time). The addresses stay in this file only: they are never printed, never put in the CSV, and the form never sends them anywhere; Maps receives them only on that tap. Leave them blank if you prefer.
How a token is earnedOne token for all the rules: at each checkpoint, one token when every rule was followed since the last one (the rules in a row, the tokens along the bottom, each slot with its checkpoint under it). Or each rule its own token: a row of tokens for each rule (up to four rules, up to six checkpoints), so a missed rule leaves only its own slot empty and the others still earn; the Tokens page and the token sheet then hold a token for every slot.
When the tokens comeSpread over the ride: the ride less the minutes kept before the stop (one to five), divided by the number of tokens, so the last token comes just before the stop, as the student nears the item; the times are rounded to the quarter minute (4:30, 9:15…). Or at a set interval (every 2 to 15 minutes): on a long ride the board fills more than once, with an exchange each time; Setup says how many times it fills, which tokens are left over before the stop, and which intervals come out even.
The goalThe stops are fixed, so a missed checkpoint cannot be made up later in the ride: with every token needed, one miss means no item that ride. While the board is new, a goal of most of the tokens (4 of 5) keeps the item within reach; it prints under the Earn box (“with 4 of 5”) and on the ride plan. Raise it to every token as the rides go well.
Fading the timerStep 1 is a timer at the checkpoint times (a vibrating watch, or a phone on vibrate). Step 2 makes the checkpoints landmarks the student can see from the window, listed in route order with the minute each is passed (a photo of the real place helps a student who does not read); the landmarks then set the number of tokens. Step 3 keeps every other landmark (the last one always), and after that the board at the stop only, then praise alone. If the rides get harder, go back a step. Setup warns when the landmarks are unevenly spaced or the last one is far from the stop.
The itemAt the stop: the board goes with the student to the adult who meets the bus, who gives the item right away when the goal is met (tell that adult beforehand what the item is and where it is kept). Or on the bus, as soon as the board is full; a non-food item is the usual choice (a sticker, a song, a little time with a tablet), and food only where the district’s transportation rules and the student’s health plan allow it.
The ride planA portrait page for the bus staff, printed after the book’s pages: the route drawn plainly (the start, the checkpoints where they fall in the ride, the stop; no map and no street), the rules with their pictures, when the tokens come, what to do at each checkpoint (a token right away with praise that names the rule; no token when a rule was not followed, the earned tokens stay, and the next checkpoint is a fresh chance), that the aide or monitor runs the board and never the driver while driving, the item, the fading steps with the current one marked, a note for the staff, and a log of the rides. Untick it on Setup to leave it out.

Load simulator on a bus book loads Sam’s sample bus ride: 25 minutes from school to home, three bus rules, five landmarks (a grocery store, the park, a fire station, the library, the bridge), the sticker to earn and five stars; nothing in it is real.

Walkthrough (the last button under View) plays a narrated walkthrough of the book in use, about three and a half minutes long, drawn from this book’s own pages, pictures and tokens: the learner’s hand picks a choice, your hand picks the target, the two cards go under First and Then, a token is given at the end of each interval with brief praise (the last one the terminal token when it is on), the tokens are traded for the item as soon as the board is full, and the pictures go back for the next round. Show it to the staff and parents who will use the book; it has captions, chapters and full screen, and it never prints. On a bus-ride book it is the bus ride instead, about two and a half minutes: the board and its rules, the item in the Earn box, the route with its checkpoints, the ride itself (the bus rolls along the route as the timer runs, and each checkpoint with the rules followed earns a token), the item at the stop or on the bus, fading the timer to landmarks and to fewer landmarks, and the ride plan. On the iPad the narration starts with the tap on Play; if nothing is heard, turn the volume up and check that Sound, under the picture, is on.

In the Assessor’s Words

From the backs: a token economy “is a program in which tokens are earned for specific behaviors and later exchanged for things the learner wants”; tokens “bridge the gap between the moment the behavior happens and the moment the real reinforcer is delivered, which helps teach waiting”; and before starting, “decide how much of the behavior earns one token: how many responses, or how long”, because “this is the schedule of reinforcement, and it must not ask too much”. The backs’ text was checked against the published literature in v21.42b and revised only where it was inaccurate or incomplete; the assessor’s structure, headings and voice are kept, and every back still fits its page.

Sources for the Backs

Premack (1959) for the principle; Timberlake and Allison (1974) for the condition that the preferred activity be restricted (response deprivation); Hackenberg (2018) for token reinforcement, token conditioning and exchange schedules; Ivy, Meindl, Overley and Robson (2017) for the components a token economy should specify; Russell, Ingvarsson, Haggar and Jessel (2018) for tokens as generalized conditioned reinforcers that hold up when one backup item has lost its value; Tiger, Hanley and Hernandez (2006) and Dyer, Dunlap and Winterling (1990) for choice (preferred by learners, and lowering problem behavior), with Lerman and colleagues (1997) for its limit (choice among items already highly preferred did not raise responding); Horner and Day (1991) for a replacement behavior that is easier than the problem behavior; Cooper, Heron and Heward (2020) for schedule thinning and ratio strain.

Writing help

The text boxes of this form (the backs, the how-to steps and the credit line) show no Improve wording button: they are instructions in the assessor’s words, not a record of what was seen, which is what Check wording is written for, and they carry the book’s own marks, which a rewrite could lose. On an iPad with Apple Intelligence, Apple’s Writing Tools (select the text) can still proofread them; it is Apple’s own and works on the text as written, on the iPad or on Apple’s servers, so follow your agency’s rules for it, and check afterwards that {n}, {token}, {last}, the ** and * marks and the blank lines between paragraphs are still there.

About the Simulator

Load simulator (toolbar) replaces every entry with a worked example; nothing in it is real. The sample student is “Sam”, with the practice’s own cards from the picture library: the choices Color, Ball, Playground, Break, YouTube and iPad (the photo), and the targets Writing, Reading, All Done, Raise hand, Math and Waiting; the smiling star is the token, and the QR code carries a sample link. The Walkthrough shows the same cards for a book whose Choices or Targets are still empty.
